plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 13: Structure Determination: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a correlation chart mapping carbon-13 chemical shifts to functional-group environments, drawn as a stack of horizontal bars over a pale yellow gradient field. The horizontal axis is labeled "Chemical shift (delta)" and reads from 220 at the left down to 0 at the right, with labeled ticks every 20 units and the unit "ppm" printed past the zero; faint vertical gridlines rise from each tick. The vertical axis carries only the word "Intensity" beside a magenta arrow pointing up, so bar height records no measured quantity and simply keeps the ranges from overlapping. Each shaded gray bar spans the shift range where one kind of carbon absorbs and carries its label. From the bottom of the stack upward these read "C=O", stretching from 220 to about 160; "C=C", roughly 150 to 107; "Aromatic", just above it over a similar span; a short "C(triple bond)N" bar near 130 to 120; "C(triple bond)C" near 95 to 80; "C-O" near 88 to 68; "C-N" near 78 to 55; a long "C-Hal" bar reaching from about 80 down to 10; then "-CH-" near 60 to 42, "-CH2-" near 50 to 28, and "-CH3" near 30 to 18 at the top. Laying every bar against one shared shift scale lets the reader see that carbons bonded to oxygen, nitrogen, or halogen fall well to the left of ordinary alkane carbons, which is what makes the chart usable for assigning the resonances of an unknown.

interactionPlan.concept: Carbon-13 chemical shifts fall into broad, overlapping ranges characteristic of each carbon environment, so a peak's position on the reversed δ scale narrows an assignment to a family of possibilities rather than naming one group outright.

interactions.label: Observed peak position (δ, ppm)
interactions.teaches: A single observed 13C peak can be consistent with several carbon environments at once, because the characteristic ranges overlap; the cursor shows exactly which families are still in play.
Each functional group occupies a definite ppm window, and groups whose carbon is bonded to O, N, or halogen sit at higher δ (farther left) because those electronegative atoms deshield the carbon.

demo_steps.title: Read the reversed scale
demo_steps.narration: The axis runs backwards: 220 ppm on the left, 0 ppm on the right. Every gray bar marks the window where one kind of carbon absorbs; bar height is only stacking, not intensity.

demo_steps.title: Alkane country (10–40 ppm)
demo_steps.narration: Park the cursor near 25 ppm and only the plain sp3 bars — CH3, CH2, and C—Hal — light up. Unsubstituted carbons hug the right end of the chart.

demo_steps.title: A crowded, ambiguous region (70 ppm)
demo_steps.narration: At 70 ppm the cursor cuts C—O, C—N, C—Hal, C≡C, and —CH— all at once. One peak here does not identify a group; it narrows the field and you need other evidence to choose.

demo_steps.title: The sp2 / aromatic band (125 ppm)
demo_steps.narration: Slide left to 125 ppm and the alkane bars go dark while C=C, Aromatic, and C≡N light up. Doubly bonded and ring carbons cluster in a band of their own.

demo_steps.title: Carbonyl carbons stand alone
demo_steps.narration: Past 160 ppm only C=O remains. A peak above 160 ppm is nearly diagnostic — the most deshielded carbon in an ordinary organic molecule is the one double-bonded to oxygen.

demo_steps.title: Inspect one band
demo_steps.narration: Hover any bar to read its endpoints and see its window projected onto the axis. Compare C—Hal's huge span against CH3's narrow one: some environments are far more diagnostic than others.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A 13C chemical shift is an overlapping range, not an address: the farther left (higher δ) a carbon appears, the more it has been deshielded by π bonding or an electronegative neighbor, and assignment means intersecting that position with every band it touches.

authoredContext:
At its simplest, 13C NMR makes it possible to count the number of different carbon atoms in a molecule. Look at the 13C NMR spectra of methyl acetate and 1-pentanol shown previously in the figureb and the figureb. In each case, a single sharp resonance line is observed for each different carbon atom.

Most 13C resonances are between 0 and 220 ppm downfield from the TMS reference line, with the exact chemical shift of each 13C resonance dependent on that carbon’s electronic environment within the molecule. The figure shows the correlation of chemical shift with environment.

The factors that determine chemical shifts are complex, but it’s possible to make some generalizations from the data in the figure. One trend is that a carbon atom’s chemical shift is affected by the electronegativity of nearby atoms. Carbons bonded to oxygen, nitrogen, or halogen absorb downfield (to the left) of typical alkane carbons. Because electronegative atoms attract electrons, they pull electrons away from neighboring carbon atoms, causing those carbons to be deshielded and to come into resonance at a lower field.

Strategy Identify the distinct carbons in the molecule, and note whether each is alkyl, vinylic, aromatic, or in a carbonyl group. Then predict where each absorbs, using the figure as necessary.

discrepancies: The magenta 'Intensity' arrow is much shorter than in the source, where it spans most of the panel height and dominates the left margin; here it is a small stub next to a small rotated 'Intensity' label.
An extra magenta annotation 'deshielded ← higher δ' appears under the left end of the axis; nothing like this exists in the source figure.

At the rendered inline size the 1200-unit viewBox scales down to ~500 px, so axis numerals, 'ppm', 'Chemical shift (δ)' and the band labels read at roughly 7–8 px — noticeably smaller/fainter than the large serif type in the source.
Minor band-extent differences: C—Hal is drawn 10–80 ppm whereas the source bar reaches ~85 ppm on the left, and C≡C/C—O endpoints are slightly narrower than the source bars.
Bands are drawn with rounded corners (radius 2) and a hover stroke, whereas source bars are plain square-cornered rectangles (cosmetic only).
evaluation.notes: A close, well-ordered reproduction of the ¹³C chemical-shift range chart with correct reversed axis, band stacking and labels, backed by a genuinely useful cursor/slider + 6-step demo; weaknesses are the shrunken intensity arrow, an invented magenta axis annotation, and small effective text size at inline scale.
action_items: Lengthen the magenta intensity arrow so it spans most of the panel height as in the source, and enlarge the rotated 'Intensity' label to match the source's prominence.
Remove (or move into the side panel) the 'deshielded ← higher δ' magenta text, which is not present in the source and clutters the axis region.
Reduce the viewBox width (or increase font sizes ~1.5×) so axis numerals and band labels remain comfortably legible when the figure is scaled into the narrow inline column.
Extend the C—Hal band to ~85 ppm and re-check C≡C / C—O endpoints against the source bar extents; drop the corner radius so bars are square like the original.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; the remaining issues are concrete rendering fixes (arrow length, hallucinated annotation, font sizing, band extents, corner radius) with no plan-level action items.

discrepancies: All text in the generated figure is rendered noticeably smaller relative to the plot than in the source (band labels ~12.5px inside an 820-unit viewBox that displays at ~520px, so effectively ~8px); the source's band labels are prominent and easily read, here they are cramped inside the bars.
Subscript numerals in —CH₂— and —CH₃ render as very small, low-baseline glyphs that read almost like commas at the displayed scale, unlike the clean subscripts in the source.

The source uses drawn bond strokes/typographic double- and triple-bond glyphs (C═O, C═C, C≡C with long bond rules and flanking line segments); the generated labels use plain '=' and em-dashes, so the chemical-structure look of the labels is slightly flattened.

Bar heights are thinner relative to row spacing than in the source, giving the stack a slightly airier, less chunky appearance; overall chart occupies a smaller share of the canvas than the source's near-full-width panel.
evaluation.notes: A close, well-composed reproduction of the ¹³C shift-range chart with correct band positions, reversed axis, magenta intensity arrow and gradient panel, plus genuinely useful interactions (draggable δ cursor, slider, 6-step guided tour, per-band popups); the main weakness is that all label text renders uncomfortably small at inline size and subscripts are poorly formed.

feedback.rationale: The concept, structure, and interactions are correct; remaining issues are purely implementation details (text sizing, subscript rendering, bond typography, bar proportions) best fixed in generation.

Side panel list titled 'Carbons that absorb here' that fills with the names of bars intersected by the cursor

interactions.label: Observed peak position (δ, ppm)
interactions.teaches: A single observed 13C peak can be consistent with several carbon environments at once, because the characteristic ranges overlap; the cursor shows exactly which families are still in play.
Each functional group occupies a definite ppm window, and groups whose carbon is bonded to O, N, or halogen sit at higher δ (farther left) because those electronegative atoms deshield the carbon.

demo_steps.title: Read the reversed scale
demo_steps.narration: The axis runs backwards: 220 ppm on the left, 0 ppm on the right. Every gray bar marks the window where one kind of carbon absorbs; bar height is only stacking, not intensity.

demo_steps.title: Alkane country (10–40 ppm)
demo_steps.narration: Park the cursor near 25 ppm and only the plain sp3 bars — CH3, CH2, and C—Hal — light up. Unsubstituted carbons hug the right end of the chart.

demo_steps.title: A crowded, ambiguous region (70 ppm)
demo_steps.narration: At 70 ppm the cursor cuts C—O, C—N, C—Hal, C≡C, and —CH— all at once. One peak here does not identify a group; it narrows the field and you need other evidence to choose.

demo_steps.title: The sp2 / aromatic band (125 ppm)
demo_steps.narration: Slide left to 125 ppm and the alkane bars go dark while C=C, Aromatic, and C≡N light up. Doubly bonded and ring carbons cluster in a band of their own.

demo_steps.title: Carbonyl carbons stand alone
demo_steps.narration: Past 160 ppm only C=O remains. A peak above 160 ppm is nearly diagnostic — the most deshielded carbon in an ordinary organic molecule is the one double-bonded to oxygen.

demo_steps.title: Inspect one band
demo_steps.narration: Hover any bar to read its endpoints and see its window projected onto the axis. Compare C—Hal's huge span against CH3's narrow one: some environments are far more diagnostic than others.

plan.keyInsight: A 13C chemical shift is an overlapping range, not an address: the farther left (higher δ) a carbon appears, the more it has been deshielded by π bonding or an electronegative neighbor, and assignment means intersecting that position with every band it touches.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Wide landscape figure. Pale yellow-to-white vertical gradient fills the plotting panel, thin dark rule around it. Axis under the panel is reversed (220 left → 0 right) with labeled ticks every 20 ppm, faint light-gray vertical gridlines through the panel, axis title 'Chemical shift (δ)' centered below and 'ppm' just right of the 0 tick. Left side: rotated word 'Intensity' with a bold magenta upward arrow, no numbers — make clear that vertical position is only stacking. Eleven warm gray-beige rounded rectangles of uniform height, each horizontally positioned by its ppm span and stacked lowest-to-highest as: C=O (220–160), C=C (150–107), Aromatic (148–110), C≡N (130–120), C≡C (95–80), C—O (88–68), C—N (78–55), C—Hal (80–10), —CH— (60–42), —CH2— (50–28), —CH3 (30–18). Serif dark labels centered inside bars; short bars use small flanking dashes as in the original. Interactive layer: a vertical cursor line (magenta, matching the arrow) with a drag handle and a δ value bubble at the top; bars it crosses switch to a saturated highlight fill with darker outline while non-intersected bars fade to low opacity. A right-hand or lower-right list panel names the currently intersected groups. Hovering a bar shows a small tooltip '92–80 ppm' style readout and paints a translucent band of the same color down over the axis strip between the two endpoints, with dotted drop lines to the tick scale. Include a small caption near the left of the axis reading 'deshielded ← higher δ' to reinforce the reversed direction.

discrepancies: Bond glyphs are simplified: the source uses proper double/triple-bond typography (C═O, C═C) with the bond line drawn as a rule, while the generated labels use plain '=' characters (C=O, C=C); the '—CH—', '—CH₂—' dashes are closer but still thinner than the source's bond strokes.
Bar rows are separated by visible vertical gaps and bars are proportionally shorter/thinner than in the source, where the stacked bands nearly touch and read as a denser staircase.

The C≡C band label in the source sits on a bar that extends slightly further left (≈95→80 ppm with the label centred); in the generated figure the small bars (C≡N, C≡C) are noticeably narrower relative to the panel, making their text sit nearly edge-to-edge with a white halo not present in the source.
Axis tick text and the 'ppm'/'Chemical shift (δ)' labels render smaller relative to the panel than in the source, where the numerals are large and prominent.
evaluation.notes: Very faithful reproduction of the ¹³C chemical-shift range chart with all 11 bands at correct ppm windows, reversed axis, magenta intensity arrow and warm gradient panel, plus a strong set of genuinely pedagogical interactions (δ cursor slider/drag, six-step guided tour, per-band popups); weaknesses are minor typographic/proportion differences (plain '=' instead of bond glyphs, thinner bars with gaps, slightly small tick text).
action_items: Render double/triple bonds as the source does — short horizontal rules (or proper ═/≡ glyphs sized to match) between atom letters for C═O, C═C, C—Hal, —CH₃, so the labels read as structural fragments rather than equations.
Increase bar height and reduce inter-row gaps so the stacked bands nearly abut as in the source, and bump axis tick/label font size a couple of points for inline legibility.
Avoid the white text halo on narrow bars by widening the bar padding or nudging the label; the source keeps all labels fully inside solid bars with no outline.
Consider matching the source's plain 'C≡C'/'C≡N' bar widths precisely (95–80 and 130–120) and verifying the drawn pixel extents against the source gridlines.
